result: The study found a non-linear relationship between sleep regularity (measured by SRI) and all-cause mortality, with irregular sleep (low SRI) associated with significantly increased mortality risk. Participants at the 5th percentile of SRI (41) had a hazard ratio of 1.53 (95% CI: 1.41, 1.66) compared to the median, while those at the 95th percentile (75) had an HR of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.81, 1.00).
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. Reviewer 1 stated the manuscript provides 'fundamental findings' with 'convincing' data quality. Reviewer 2 noted the analysis 'reported robust associations between sleep irregularity and increased total...mortality' and that 'the data quality and large sample size strengthen the credibility of the conclusion.' No reviewer questioned the statistical findings or methodology for all-cause mortality.

result: The SRI was significantly associated with CVD-specific mortality (p<0.001), with a hazard ratio of 1.88 (95% CI: 1.61, 2.21) for the 5th percentile relative to the median. The association showed proportional hazards over time and was stronger in females than males (p interaction = 0.006).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly stated the analysis 'reported robust associations between sleep irregularity and increased...CVD...mortality.' Reviewer 1 noted the findings will be of 'wide interest' and the data quality is 'convincing.' No reviewer challenged the CVD mortality findings or the sex-specific effects.

result: The SRI was associated with cancer mortality (p<0.001), with a hazard ratio of 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22, 1.53) for the 5th percentile relative to the median. However, the association showed non-proportional hazards over time, with hazard ratios declining from >2 at baseline to ~1.05 after 4 years.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirmed 'robust associations between sleep irregularity and increased...cancer mortality.' The time-varying nature of the cancer mortality association was not questioned by any reviewer, though Reviewer 3 raised concerns about causality more broadly (discussed separately). The statistical findings themselves were accepted.

result: The associations between SRI and mortality remained significant after adjusting for multiple confounders including sleep duration, WASO, disease history, BMI, blood pressure, and physical activity, though effect sizes were attenuated in the fully adjusted model (Model 4).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'the analyses are appropriately done' and praised the robustness of the findings. Reviewer 1 stated the 'data quality and large sample size are convincing and strengthen the credibility of the conclusion.' No reviewer questioned the sensitivity analyses or adjustment strategy.

result: The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) was superior to standard deviation-based metrics (sleep duration SD and sleep onset time SD) in predicting mortality. The SRI improved model fit when added to SD-based metrics (p<0.001), but SD metrics did not improve fit when added to SRI models (p=0.10).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlighted that 'The Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) used in this study is a novel metric that quantifies the consistency in rest-activity rhythms over consecutive 24 hour periods, thus providing objective assessment of potential circadian disruption.' The comparative superiority of SRI over SD-based metrics was not challenged by any reviewer.

result: Time-varying hazard analysis revealed that for all-cause mortality, hazard ratios for low SRI (5th percentile) were highest early in follow-up (HRs >2), declining until ~2.5 years, then stabilizing at HR ~1.5.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the time-varying hazard findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 stated 'Overall, the analyses are appropriately done' and Reviewer 1 found the data 'convincing.' The statistical methodology for time-varying effects was not questioned.

result: The authors acknowledge the observational study design limits causal inference. They suggest irregular sleep may be a manifestation of cancer itself (reverse causation) but note that a causal role for irregular sleep on CVD death cannot be easily ruled out.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raised this concern, stating 'the analysis can not to accurately identify the cause and effect' and that 'causality is important for this topic' given that 'sleep regularity and health...were long-term simultaneous status.' Reviewer 3 suggested 'the author could utilize MR analysis to find out for more evidence,' indicating the causal interpretation remains uncertain.

result: The study analyzed 88,975 UK Biobank participants (mean age 62 years, 56% women, median SRI 60) with 7-day accelerometry data, documenting 3,010 deaths over 7.1 years of follow-up, with cancer (57%) and CVD (20%) as the most common causes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The study is based on a large accelerometer study with validated follow-up of incident diseases and deaths, and the data quality and large sample size are convincing.' Reviewer 2 similarly noted 'The data quality and large sample size strengthen the credibility of the conclusion.' No reviewer questioned the cohort characteristics or data quality.

result: Accelerometry data were collected using wrist-worn devices and processed using the GGIR algorithm, which identifies a main sleep period time window but does not detect napping. The authors acknowledge this methodological limitation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted that accelerometry 'providing objective assessment of potential circadian disruption' and that 'the analyses are appropriately done.' No reviewer challenged the accelerometry methodology or the GGIR algorithm, though the limitation regarding nap detection was acknowledged by the authors and not disputed.

result: Mortality was ascertained through NHS linkage with complete records until January 2022. Cox proportional hazards models with restricted cubic splines were used for analysis, with missing data (<2%) imputed by predictive mean matching.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'validated follow-up of incident diseases and deaths' and Reviewer 2 stated 'the analyses are appropriately done.' The statistical methodology was not questioned by any reviewer.

result: The manuscript provides background on circadian rhythms, their regulation by light exposure, and associations between circadian disruption and age-related diseases including cancer and CVD. It contextualizes the study within existing literature on sleep-wake variability and health outcomes.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted the manuscript 'provided evidence to support the role of sleep and circadian health in disease progression and longevity in human populations' and that it is 'a popular topic in recent sleep and circadian research.' The background and contextualization were accepted without challenge.

result: The authors conclude that these data indicate a relationship between sleep regularity and longevity in a large community-based cohort.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated the findings will be 'of wide interest to researchers in the sleep study field, epidemiologists, practicing clinicians and the general public.' Reviewer 2 noted the study 'provided evidence to support the role of sleep and circadian health in disease progression and longevity.' The overall conclusion was affirmed by reviewers despite the causality concerns raised separately.
